lead: A two-port is a box with an input port and an output port. Z parameters describe it by writing the two port voltages as sums of terms proportional to the two port currents. Y parameters do the opposite: they write the two port currents in terms of the two port voltages. Both descriptions carry the same information, because the Y matrix is the inverse of the Z matrix. Data sheets of transformers, filters and small RF blocks quote them. They also let you combine networks: series connections add Z matrices and parallel connections add Y matrices (see 6.6).
prereq: You need: 6.1 for the four port variables V₁, I₁, V₂, I₂, Ohm's law and KVL/KCL from Unit 1, and impedance from Unit 3.

blocks.text: Z parameters, also called open-circuit impedance parameters, treat the two port currents I₁ and I₂ as the causes and the two port voltages V₁ and V₂ as the effects. Both currents enter their ports, following the sign convention fixed in 6.1. The network is linear, so the relations are linear.
V₁ = z₁₁I₁ + z₁₂I₂    and    V₂ = z₂₁I₁ + z₂₂I₂
blocks.where: I₁, I₂ are the port currents in amperes, entering the top terminals; V₁, V₂ are the port voltages in volts; z₁₁, z₁₂, z₂₁, z₂₂ are the Z parameters, each in ohms (V/A). The four numbers form the matrix Z = [[z₁₁, z₁₂], [z₂₁, z₂₂]].

blocks.text: To isolate z₁₁ you must make I₂ zero, which means leaving port 2 open. Then V₁ = z₁₁I₁, so z₁₁ = V₁/I₁. It is simply the input impedance seen at port 1 with the output open. In that same test V₂ = z₂₁I₁, so z₂₁ = V₂/I₁: the voltage appearing at port 2 for each ampere pushed into port 1.

Swap the roles for the other two. Open port 1 so I₁ = 0, drive port 2, and read V₂ = z₂₂I₂ and V₁ = z₁₂I₂. Here z₂₂ = V₂/I₂ is the output impedance with the input open, and z₁₂ = V₁/I₂ is the transfer impedance measured backwards. An ohmmeter placed on one port with the other left open reads the diagonal terms directly.

items: Apply a known test current I₁ at port 1.
Compute z₁₁ = V₁/I₁ and z₂₁ = V₂/I₁, both in ohms.
Open port 1, drive port 2, and compute z₁₂ = V₁/I₂ and z₂₂ = V₂/I₂ the same way.

blocks.text: Y parameters, or short-circuit admittance parameters, turn the equations around: voltages now drive and currents respond.
I₁ = y₁₁V₁ + y₁₂V₂    and    I₂ = y₂₁V₁ + y₂₂V₂
blocks.where: V₁, V₂ are the port voltages in volts; I₁, I₂ are the port currents in amperes; y₁₁, y₁₂, y₂₁, y₂₂ are the Y parameters, each in siemens (A/V), written S. The matrix is Y = [[y₁₁, y₁₂], [y₂₁, y₂₂]].

blocks.text: Set V₂ = 0 by short-circuiting port 2. Then I₁ = y₁₁V₁, so y₁₁ = I₁/V₁ is the input admittance with the output shorted. Also I₂ = y₂₁V₁, so y₂₁ = I₂/V₁ is the short-circuit transfer admittance. Short port 1 instead (V₁ = 0) and drive port 2 to get y₁₂ = I₁/V₂ and y₂₂ = I₂/V₂.
Because the two sets describe the same box, Y is the matrix inverse of Z.
y₁₁ = z₂₂/Δz,  y₁₂ = −z₁₂/Δz,  y₂₁ = −z₂₁/Δz,  y₂₂ = z₁₁/Δz,  where Δz = z₁₁z₂₂ − z₁₂z₂₁
blocks.where: Δz is the determinant of the Z matrix, in Ω². Each y comes out in S.

blocks.text: Watch the signs. The diagonal terms keep their sign, but both off-diagonal terms pick up a minus sign from the inverse. And z₁₂ is not 1/y₁₂: the inverse of a matrix is not the matrix of reciprocals.

sections.h3: Which set exists, and which to use

items: Z needs a good open circuit at the far port; Y needs a good short. At high frequency stray capacitance spoils an open, so RF engineers prefer short-circuit tests or scattering parameters.

If Δz = 0 the Z matrix is singular and no Y matrix exists. A passive T network of ordinary elements never hits this, but an ideal transformer does: it forces V₁ = nV₂ and I₁ = −I₂/n, so the port variables are not free and neither a Z nor a Y matrix can be written. The transmission parameters of 6.4 handle it.
A reciprocal network has z₁₂ = z₂₁ and y₁₂ = y₂₁; a symmetric one has z₁₁ = z₂₂ and y₁₁ = y₂₂. See 6.7.
Conversion to h or ABCD parameters is pure algebra on the same two equations; see 6.5.

figure.caption: The chain starts with the open-circuit test that gives z₁₁, then repeats the same two-port with port 2 shorted to give y₁₁. Notice that only the port condition changes between the two halves.

spec.title: Z test then Y test
spec.aria: A downward chain: open port 2, apply I₁, measure V₁ and get z₁₁; then short port 2, apply V₁, measure I₁ and get y₁₁.

examples.question: A T network has a series arm Z₁ = 2 Ω on the port 1 side, a series arm Z₂ = 3 Ω on the port 2 side, and a shunt arm Z₃ = 4 Ω from the centre node to the common return. (a) Find z₁₁, z₁₂, z₂₁ and z₂₂. (b) Find Δz and all four Y parameters. (c) Find the input impedance with port 2 shorted and compare it with z₁₁.
steps: With port 2 open, I₂ = 0, so no current flows in Z₂. The current I₁ passes through Z₁ and Z₃ in series: V₁ = I₁(Z₁ + Z₃) = I₁(2 + 4) = 6I₁, giving z₁₁ = 6 Ω.
The same current develops V₂ across Z₃ only: V₂ = I₁Z₃ = 4I₁, giving z₂₁ = 4 Ω.
With port 1 open, I₁ = 0 and I₂ passes through Z₂ and Z₃: V₂ = I₂(Z₂ + Z₃) = I₂(3 + 4) = 7I₂, giving z₂₂ = 7 Ω.
The same I₂ develops V₁ across Z₃: V₁ = I₂Z₃ = 4I₂, giving z₁₂ = 4 Ω. Since z₁₂ = z₂₁, the network is reciprocal.

With port 2 shorted, Z₂ and Z₃ are in parallel: their combination is (3)(4)/(3 + 4) = 1.7143 Ω, and the input impedance is Z₁ + 1.7143 = 2 + 1.7143 = 3.7143 Ω. This is not z₁₁ = 6 Ω, because the port condition is different.
examples.answer: z₁₁ = 6 Ω, z₁₂ = z₂₁ = 4 Ω, z₂₂ = 7 Ω; Δz = 26 Ω²; y₁₁ = 0.2692 S, y₁₂ = y₂₁ = −0.1538 S, y₂₂ = 0.2308 S; input impedance with port 2 shorted is 3.7143 Ω.

traps: z₁₁ is not measured with port 2 shorted. For the example network, shorting port 2 gives 3.7143 Ω, not 6 Ω. Z parameters always need an open circuit; Y parameters always need a short circuit.
z₁₂ is not 1/y₁₂. Here z₁₂ = 4 Ω while 1/y₁₂ = 1/(−0.1538) = −6.5 Ω. The inverse of a matrix is not the matrix of reciprocals.
Sign slip: y₁₂ and y₂₁ carry a minus sign from the inverse; z₁₂ and z₂₁ do not. Writing y₁₂ = +z₁₂/Δz is the most common lost mark.
Units: Z parameters in ohms, Y parameters in siemens, Δz in Ω². A determinant written in plain ohms loses a mark.
Forcing a matrix on a network that has none: an ideal transformer has no finite Z or Y matrix, because its ports are not independent. Use ABCD parameters there.

quiz.q: Define z₁₂ and give its test condition, unit and physical meaning.
quiz.a: z₁₂ = V₁/I₂ with I₁ = 0, that is port 1 open and port 2 driven. Unit: ohm. It is the voltage produced at port 1 per ampere driven into port 2.

quiz.q: Why are Z parameters called open-circuit parameters and Y parameters called short-circuit parameters?
quiz.a: Each Z parameter is found with the far port open (current zero), so the test is an open-circuit test. Each Y parameter is found with the far port shorted (voltage zero), so the test is a short-circuit test.

quiz.q: A two-port has y₁₁ = 0.2692 S and y₂₁ = −0.1538 S. Why is y₂₁ negative for a passive network?
quiz.a: y₂₁ = −z₂₁/Δz. The transfer impedance z₂₁ is positive, but the matrix inverse puts a minus sign on the off-diagonal term, so a passive network can still give a negative transfer admittance.

quiz.q: A two-port has z₁₁ = 10 Ω, z₁₂ = z₂₁ = 5 Ω, z₂₂ = 20 Ω. Find Δz and y₁₁.
For the T network of the worked example, find the output impedance seen at port 2 with port 1 shorted. Compare it with z₂₂.
quiz.a: With port 1 shorted, Z₁ and Z₃ are in parallel: (2)(4)/(2 + 4) = 1.3333 Ω. Add Z₂: 3 + 1.3333 = 4.3333 Ω. This is not z₂₂ = 7 Ω, because the port condition differs.

quiz.q: For a general T network with arms Z₁, Z₂ and Z₃, prove that Δz = Z₁Z₂ + Z₁Z₃ + Z₂Z₃, and state when the Y matrix fails to exist.
quiz.a: Use z₁₁ = Z₁ + Z₃, z₁₂ = z₂₁ = Z₃, z₂₂ = Z₂ + Z₃. Then Δz = (Z₁ + Z₃)(Z₂ + Z₃) − Z₃² = Z₁Z₂ + Z₁Z₃ + Z₂Z₃. The Y matrix fails only when Δz = 0. For a passive T network built from positive resistors this sum is positive, so Y always exists; degenerate cases such as an ideal transformer have no Z matrix at all.

beyond: Not for the exam. Above a few hundred megahertz, a wire stub or a stray capacitor ruins the open and short circuits that Z and Y tests rely on. Radio engineers instead measure scattering (S) parameters with a vector network analyzer, then convert to Z or Y when they need them. Search for "S parameters", "vector network analyzer" and "two-port Y parameters of a Π network" to see the same algebra in microwave form.
